column1: You run dnf install filebeat and get 'GPG check FAILED'. The repo file exists and gpgcheck=1. What was skipped and what is the fix?
column2: The GPG key was never imported. The repo file's gpgkey= line tells dnf where to find the key but does not import it automatically. Fix: sudo rpm --import https://repo-url/GPG-KEY then retry install. On Debian: curl -fsSL URL | gpg --dearmor | sudo tee /etc/apt/keyrings/name.gpg

column1: rpm -V openssh-clients returns: S.5....T.  /usr/bin/ssh (no c tag). What does this mean and how serious is it?
column2: Size (S), MD5 hash (5), and mtime (T) all differ from the package database record. No 'c' tag means this is a regular binary — not a config file. A modified ssh binary with no distro update to explain it is a serious security indicator. Remediation: check dnf history for a legitimate update. If none found, isolate host, preserve for forensics, reinstall: dnf reinstall openssh-clients

column1: What is the difference between apt remove and apt purge? When do you use each?
column2: apt remove uninstalls binaries but leaves config files. apt purge removes binaries AND config files. Use remove when you may reinstall and want to keep config. Use purge for a clean slate — reinstalling fresh, or permanent removal. In containers and CI, always purge to avoid config residue affecting subsequent installs.

column1: A Kubernetes worker node's kubelet upgraded unexpectedly from 1.29 to 1.30 during dnf upgrade. Node is NotReady. What should have been done after the initial install?
column2: dnf versionlock add kubelet kubeadm kubectl (RHEL) or apt-mark hold kubelet kubeadm kubectl (Ubuntu). All three packages must be version-locked together — they must stay in lockstep with the control plane. The lock is released, upgrade performed at planned version, then re-applied.

column1: Why must apt-get update and apt-get install be in the same RUN instruction in a Dockerfile?
column2: Docker caches each RUN layer. If they are separate, a future build uses the cached update layer (stale index) but re-runs install — installing whatever version the stale index knows, not the latest. This is cache busting failure causing non-reproducible builds. One RUN layer ensures the index is always fresh when packages install.

column1: What does --no-install-recommends do in apt-get install? Why use it in containers?
column2: Prevents installation of recommended packages — packages not strictly required for the tool to function. apt installs recommended packages by default. In a container, recommended packages add size with no benefit. Typical image size reduction: 20-40%. Always use --no-install-recommends in Dockerfiles.

column1: rpm -V nginx returns nothing. rpm -V nginx shows: .M.......  /usr/sbin/nginx. What does each mean?
column2: No output: all files match the package database — package is intact. .M.......: the M position (mode/permissions) differs from the database record. Permissions on the nginx binary were changed after install. Investigate: was this intentional hardening? Run stat /usr/sbin/nginx to see current permissions. May be benign but warrants review.

column1: What is the relationship between apt and dpkg? Between dnf and rpm?
column2: apt is the high-level tool: resolves dependencies, fetches packages from repos, then calls dpkg to install. dpkg is the low-level tool: installs/removes .deb files, manages the package database, does NOT resolve deps. Same relationship: dnf (high-level) calls rpm (low-level). Use high-level for install/remove. Use low-level for queries (dpkg -S, rpm -qf) and verification (rpm -V).

column1: What is the difference between a binary package and a source package? Which does apt/dnf install by default?
column2: Binary package: pre-compiled, ready to install as-is — what apt/dnf install by default (e.g. nginx, curl, jq). Source package: contains source code you compile yourself for your exact system (Debian: .dsc + .orig.tar.* + .debian.tar.*; RHEL: .src.rpm). Source packages are rare in day-to-day DevOps work — mainly used when no binary exists for your architecture or you need a custom compile-time option.

column1: What is a meta-package? Give an example use case.
column2: A meta-package contains no files of its own — it exists purely to pull in a group of other packages as dependencies. Example: a build-essential-style package that depends on gcc, make, and related tools, giving you one thing to install instead of several.

A name a package manager recognizes that isn't a real package itself — it represents a capability that multiple real packages can satisfy. Example: several different mail-server packages can all 'provide' mail-transport-agent, letting other packages depend on the capability rather than one specific implementation.

column1: Is a package's embedded metadata the same thing as a repository's package index? Explain the difference.
column2: No. A package's metadata (name, version, dependencies, maintainer) is embedded inside that one package file and describes only itself. The repository index (Packages/Release for Debian, repodata for RHEL) is a separate manifest the repository publishes, built by aggregating metadata across every package it hosts, plus a checksum for each entry. The index is what search/show/info query before install; the package's own metadata is read from the local install database after install.

column1: A package manager installs nginx via apt. Where do the binary, config, logs, and persistent data each go, and why does this match Demo 01's FHS map rather than a separate 'package manager' convention?
column2: Binary: /usr/bin/nginx (package-manager-installed binaries). Config: /etc/nginx/ (host-specific service config). Logs: /var/log/nginx/ (persistent growing log data). Data: /var/lib/nginx/ (persistent app state). The package manager doesn't invent new locations — it follows the exact FHS map from Demo 01. This is the 'package manager install' pattern, distinct from manual install (/usr/local/bin only) and vendor self-contained install (/opt, everything together).

column1: Why does this demo's Dockerfile NOT pin exact package versions like curl=8.5.0-2ubuntu10.6, even though pinning is described as good practice for reproducibility?
column2: Ubuntu publishes frequent security patch rebuilds that change the patch suffix every few weeks. A hardcoded version string copied from documentation or an earlier build can simply no longer exist in the repo, causing 'Version ... was not found' errors. For general-purpose tooling images, pinning only the base image tag (ubuntu:24.04, never :latest) and leaving package versions unpinned is more maintainable. True version pinning, when genuinely required, must use a version string fetched fresh via apt-cache policy immediately before that exact build — never reused from an earlier session.
